title: Double the substrate, then what?
hook: Give an enzyme twice as much to work on. How much faster does it get?

knows: an enzyme works on one substrate molecule at a time
doesNotKnow: that reaction speed levels off when almost all enzymes are busy (saturation)
how small the gain from extra substrate is near saturation

misconception: Doubling the substrate doubles the reaction rate.
objective: The learner can explain that speed is proportional to S/(Km + S), so at 10 times the half-way concentration almost all enzymes are busy and doubling the substrate adds only about 5%, while at low substrate doubling helps far more.

claims.text: For a simple single-substrate enzyme, the half-way concentration (Km) is the substrate level at which half the enzymes are busy, and the busy share is S / (Km + S); speed is that share times the top speed (Michaelis-Menten).
claims.source: Nelson D.L. & Cox M.M., Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry, chapter on enzyme kinetics (Michaelis-Menten equation).

claims.text: At S = 10 Km, 10/11 = 91 of 100 enzymes are busy; at 20 Km, 20/21 = 95 of 100, so doubling from 10 to 20 speeds the reaction up by about 4% (95 / 91 = 1.044 from the rounded counts the stage shows; exactly 1.048).
From S = 1 Km to 2 Km, busy enzymes go from 50 to 67 of 100: about 34% faster (67 / 50 = 1.34 from the counts shown; exactly 1.333).

The 100 stations, each handling one molecule at a time with a busy share S/(Km + S), are a simplification of single-substrate kinetics; top speed is the speed when all enzymes are busy; the waiting-substrate pool is a picture, not a count.
claims.source: Drawing choice in Demo.tsx; pool positions from an untuned seed (mulberry32(9)).

recall.question: An enzyme is already almost fully busy. You triple the substrate. The reaction speed…
recall.why: Near saturation almost every enzyme is already working, so extra substrate mostly waits its turn; speed creeps toward its top rate.
